subject: chemistry

items.q: Which statement describes how a nucleophile forms a new bond to its reaction partner?
items.correct: It donates both electrons of the new covalent bond.
items.misconception: It accepts the two electrons of the new covalent bond.
items.why: 'Electro-' sounds like 'having electrons', so 'electrophile' is read as 'electron-rich'. The Greek -phile means 'loving': an electrophile loves (seeks) electrons because it is short of them, and a nucleophile seeks a positive centre (a nucleus). An electrophile is electron-seeking, so it is electron-deficient and ACCEPTS a pair. A nucleophile is nucleus-seeking, so it is electron-rich and DONATES a pair. OH⁻, H₂O, NH₃ and the C=C bond are electron-rich donors; H⁺, NO₂⁺, HBr and Br₂ act as acceptors.
items.specStatementText: A nucleophile is a reactant that forms a bond to its reaction partner (the electrophile) by donating both bonding electrons.
items.random_wrong: It gives one electron, and its partner gives the other.

items.q:
2-bromo-2-methylpropane reacts with water:
(CH₃)₃CBr + H₂O → (CH₃)₃COH + HBr
Which reactant acts as the nucleophile, and why?
items.correct: H₂O, as a lone pair on its O atom forms the new bond to carbon
items.misconception: Neither, as neither reactant carries a negative charge
items.why: The first nucleophiles students meet are anions such as OH⁻ and CN⁻, and 'attracted to positive centres' is easily read as 'must itself be negative'. Identifying nucleophiles by charge rather than by available electron pairs is widely reported in chemistry-education research on organic reaction mechanisms. Look for an available electron pair, not a charge. H₂O and NH₃ are neutral nucleophiles: each donates a lone pair to form a new bond. The nucleophile in a reaction is the species whose electron pair forms the new bond; a δ− atom that leaves, such as Br in a halogenoalkane, is the leaving group, not the nucleophile.
items.specStatementText: A nucleophile is a reactant that forms a bond to its reaction partner (the electrophile) by donating both bonding electrons.
items.random_wrong: (CH₃)₃CBr, as its C atom accepts a pair of electrons

items.q: 1-bromopropane is warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide. Which equation represents the reaction that occurs?
items.correct: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + Br⁻
items.misconception: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂CH₂⁻ + HOBr
items.why: Students associate the halogen with the 'reactive' functional group and look at the most eye-catching atom. They do not use bond polarity to find the electron-deficient atom, which is the atom an electron-rich species is attracted to. An electron-rich species is attracted to the δ+ atom, not the δ− atom. In C–Br the carbon is δ+, so OH⁻ bonds to carbon and Br leaves as Br⁻.
items.specStatementText: In a nucleophilic substitution reaction, a nucleophile donates an electron pair to form a new bond, as another bond breaks producing a leaving group.
items.random_wrong: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂CHBr⁻ + H₂O

items.q: In the reaction CH₃CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂OH + Br⁻ a new C–O bond forms. Where do the two electrons of the new C–O bond come from?
items.correct: Both from a lone pair on the O atom of the OH⁻ ion
items.misconception: One from the O atom and one from the C atom
items.why: Covalent bonding is first taught with dot-and-cross diagrams such as H₂ and Cl₂, in which each atom contributes one electron to each shared pair. The rule is then applied to every bond, including bonds made in reactions. Bonds can also form with both electrons from one partner. In nucleophile–electrophile reactions (and in coordination bonds) the donor supplies both electrons. The finished bond is still a shared pair; only its origin differs.
items.specStatementText: In a nucleophilic substitution reaction, a nucleophile donates an electron pair to form a new bond, as another bond breaks producing a leaving group.
items.random_wrong: Both from the C–Br bond, which becomes the new C–O bond

items.q: Which statement describes the heterolytic fission of a covalent bond?
items.correct: Both bonding electrons go to one fragment, so two ions form.
items.misconception: One bonding electron goes to each fragment, so radicals form.
items.why: The bond-breaking step students meet first in organic chemistry is homolytic fission of halogens under UV light in radical substitution, and the picture 'each atom takes back its own electron' matches the dot-and-cross view of a bond. It is then applied to every bond. Bonds can break in two ways. Homolytic: one electron to each fragment, giving radicals (Br–Br → 2Br•). Heterolytic: both electrons to one fragment, giving ions (H–Br → H⁺ + Br⁻; C–Br in a halogenoalkane → Br⁻ leaving). Substitution by nucleophiles involves heterolytic fission.
items.specStatementText: Heterolytic fission is the breakage of a covalent bond when both bonding electrons remain with one of the two fragments formed.
items.random_wrong: Both bonding electrons go to one fragment, which becomes positive.

items.q: Hydrogen chloride undergoes heterolytic fission to form H⁺ and Cl⁻. Which describes the curly arrow for this change?
items.correct: It starts at the H–Cl bond and ends on the Cl atom.
items.misconception: It starts at the H–Cl bond and ends on the H atom.
items.why: 'Gaining' is associated with 'plus', and students confuse the sign convention for charge with the idea of gaining something. The same sign confusion appears when oxidation and reduction are described in terms of electrons. Electrons are negative. A fragment that ends up with both bonding electrons has one more electron than it contributed, so it is negative: H–Cl → H⁺ + Cl⁻, with Cl taking the pair.
items.specStatementText: Heterolytic fission is the breakage of a covalent bond when both bonding electrons remain with one of the two fragments formed.
items.random_wrong: It starts on the Cl atom and points back to the H–Cl bond.

items.q:
Ethene reacts with bromine:
CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br
Which reactant acts as the electrophile?
items.correct: Br₂, as it accepts an electron pair from the C=C bond
items.misconception: Neither, as neither reactant carries a positive charge
items.why: The electrophiles students meet first are cations such as H⁺ and NO₂⁺, and 'electron-seeking' is easily read as 'must be positive'. Identifying electrophiles by charge rather than by the ability to accept an electron pair is widely reported in chemistry-education research. Classify by what the species does. Any species that accepts an electron pair to form a new bond is an electrophile, whether it is a cation (H⁺, NO₂⁺) or a neutral molecule (HBr, Br₂). Alkenes react readily with HBr, Br₂ and, with an acid catalyst, water. Even non-polar Br₂ acts as an electrophile: it reacts rapidly with alkenes, and loss of the orange-brown colour is the test for C=C.
items.specStatementText: An electrophile is a reactant that forms a bond to its reaction partner (the nucleophile) by accepting both bonding electrons from that reaction partner.
items.random_wrong: Ethene, as its C=C bond is rich in electrons

items.q:
Ammonia reacts with hydrogen ions:
NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺
Which species acts as the electrophile?
items.correct: H⁺, as it accepts the lone pair on the nitrogen atom
items.misconception: H⁺, as it forms an ionic bond with the nitrogen atom of NH₃
items.why: In ionic bonding students learn that metal atoms 'give' or 'donate' electrons to non-metal atoms. The same word is used for nucleophiles, so the ionic picture is carried over. In nucleophilic reactions 'donate' means 'supply for sharing'. The pair ends up shared between the nucleophile atom and the electrophile atom, forming a covalent bond, e.g. the C–O bond in CH₃CH₂OH.
items.specStatementText: An electrophile is a reactant that forms a bond to its reaction partner (the nucleophile) by accepting both bonding electrons from that reaction partner.
items.random_wrong: NH₃, as its nitrogen atom carries a lone pair of electrons

items.q: Why are alkenes susceptible to attack by electrophiles?
items.correct: The C=C double bond is a region of high electron density.
items.misconception: The C=C double bond is weaker than a C–C single bond.
items.why: 'Reactive' is equated with 'weak', and students are told that alkenes are more reactive than alkanes. They conclude that the double bond must be the weaker bond. Reactivity and bond strength are different things. C=C is stronger than C–C, yet alkenes react with electrophiles because the double bond concentrates electron density between and around the two carbon atoms, where electrophiles are attracted.
items.specStatementText: Alkenes are susceptible to electrophilic attack because of the high electron density of the carbon–carbon double bond. These reactions lead to electrophilic addition.
items.random_wrong: The carbon atoms of C=C are deficient in electrons.

items.q: Ethene is bubbled through a solution of bromine in an organic solvent at room temperature, in the dark. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: The bromine loses its colour as CH₂BrCH₂Br forms by addition.
items.misconception: The bromine loses its colour as CH₂=CHBr forms by substitution.
items.why: Students learn radical substitution of alkanes with halogens first and carry the pattern 'halogen replaces H' to all hydrocarbons. The C=C double bond is the reactive site of an alkene. The reagent adds across it: water gives an alcohol, a halogen gives a dihalogenoalkane, and a hydrogen halide gives a halogenoalkane. The product has no C=C bond.
items.specStatementText: Alkenes are susceptible to electrophilic attack because of the high electron density of the carbon–carbon double bond. These reactions lead to electrophilic addition.
items.random_wrong: No reaction occurs, as Br₂ has no positive charge.

items.q: But-2-ene, CH₃CH=CHCH₃, undergoes hydration when heated with steam in the presence of an acid catalyst. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Water adds across the C=C bond, forming butan-2-ol.
items.misconception: Water adds across the C=C bond, forming butane-2,3-diol.
items.why: The first addition reaction many students learn is with bromine, in which both carbons gain the same atom. The pattern 'same group on each carbon' is then over-generalized to H₂O and HX. Split the reagent into its two parts and add one part to each carbon: H₂O → H and OH, so ethene gives ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH; HBr → H and Br, so ethene gives bromoethane, CH₃CH₂Br. Br₂ → Br and Br gives CH₂BrCH₂Br.
items.specStatementText: Alkenes are susceptible to electrophilic attack because of the high electron density of the carbon–carbon double bond. These reactions lead to electrophilic addition.
items.random_wrong: An OH group replaces an H atom, forming but-2-en-2-ol.

items.q: Ethene is mixed with hydrogen bromide gas at room temperature. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: HBr adds across the C=C bond, forming CH₃CH₂Br.
items.misconception: HBr adds across the C=C bond, forming CH₂BrCH₂Br.
items.why: The first addition reaction many students learn is with bromine, in which both carbons gain the same atom. The pattern 'same group on each carbon' is then over-generalized to H₂O and HX. Split the reagent into its two parts and add one part to each carbon: H₂O → H and OH, so ethene gives ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH; HBr → H and Br, so ethene gives bromoethane, CH₃CH₂Br. Br₂ → Br and Br gives CH₂BrCH₂Br.
items.specStatementText: Alkenes are susceptible to electrophilic attack because of the high electron density of the carbon–carbon double bond. These reactions lead to electrophilic addition.
items.random_wrong: A Br atom replaces one H atom, forming CH₂=CHBr.

items.q:
Aluminium chloride reacts with chloride ions:
AlCl₃ + Cl⁻ → AlCl₄⁻
Which statement identifies the Lewis acid in this reaction?
items.correct: AlCl₃, as it accepts an electron pair from Cl⁻
items.misconception: Cl⁻, as it donates an electron pair to AlCl₃
items.why: In Brønsted–Lowry theory the acid is the donor (of H⁺), so students keep 'acid = donor' and attach it to the electron pair in Lewis theory. The two definitions are in fact complementary: an H⁺ donor is an electron-pair acceptor. Link the two theories through H⁺: H⁺ accepts an electron pair, so it is a Lewis acid. In Lewis terms, acid = electron-pair ACCEPTOR (H⁺, BF₃, AlCl₃, metal cations) and base = electron-pair DONOR (NH₃, H₂O, OH⁻, Cl⁻, C=C).
items.specStatementText: A Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor and a Lewis base is an electron-pair donor.
items.random_wrong: Neither, as no H⁺ ion is transferred at all

items.q: In the first step of the acid-catalysed addition of water to ethene, H⁺ bonds to one carbon atom of the C=C bond, forming CH₃CH₂⁺. Which species acts as the Lewis base in this step?
items.correct: Ethene, as its C=C electrons form the new C–H bond
items.misconception: Neither, as ethene has no lone pair to donate
items.why: Nearly every Lewis base shown in inorganic examples (NH₃, H₂O, Cl⁻) donates a lone pair, and Lewis formulas draw lone pairs prominently, so 'donor' becomes 'has a lone pair'. What matters is an available electron pair. The electron-rich second bond of C=C is donated to H⁺ in the first step of electrophilic addition, so the alkene is the Lewis base and H⁺ is the Lewis acid.
items.specStatementText: A Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor and a Lewis base is an electron-pair donor.
items.random_wrong: H⁺, as it accepts the electron pair of the C=C bond

items.q: Ammonia reacts with boron trifluoride to form H₃NBF₃. The Lewis formula of the product is often drawn with a positive formal charge on N and a negative formal charge on B. Which statement about the new N–B bond is correct?
items.correct: It is a coordination bond; both electrons came from N
items.misconception: It is an ionic bond, as N carries + and B carries −
items.why: Students associate + and − signs with ions and ionic bonding, and do not distinguish formal charges on atoms within a molecule from charges on separate ions. Formal charges show how the electrons were counted, not separate ions. H₃N–BF₃ is a single molecule in which N and B share the pair donated by nitrogen, so the N–B bond is a coordination (covalent) bond.
items.specStatementText: When a Lewis base reacts with a Lewis acid, a coordination bond is formed. Nucleophiles are Lewis bases and electrophiles are Lewis acids.
items.random_wrong: It is a coordination bond; both of its electrons came from B

items.q: In the reaction CH₃CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂OH + Br⁻, which statement about OH⁻ is correct?
items.correct: It is a nucleophile, and so it is also a Lewis base.
items.misconception: It is a nucleophile but no base, as it gains no H⁺.
items.why: Brønsted–Lowry theory, learned first, defines acids and bases entirely by proton transfer, and most familiar acids contain hydrogen. Students keep that definition when the Lewis definition is introduced. The Lewis definitions widen the idea: acid = electron-pair acceptor, base = electron-pair donor. BF₃ + NH₃ → H₃NBF₃ and AlCl₃ + Cl⁻ → AlCl₄⁻ are Lewis acid–base reactions with no proton transferred.
items.specStatementText: When a Lewis base reacts with a Lewis acid, a coordination bond is formed. Nucleophiles are Lewis bases and electrophiles are Lewis acids.
items.random_wrong: It is a nucleophile, and so it is a Lewis acid.

items.q: Which statement describes the bonding between H₂O and Cu²⁺ in the complex ion [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺?
items.correct: Each H₂O donates a lone pair to Cu²⁺, forming a coordination bond.
items.misconception: Each H₂O is held to Cu²⁺ by an ionic bond, as Cu is a metal.
items.why: The shortcut 'metal + non-metal = ionic' is taught early and works for simple salts such as NaCl, so it is applied to complex ions and to aluminium chloride as well. Decide bond type by what the electrons do, not by the elements' names. In a complex ion each ligand donates an electron pair that is shared with the metal ion (a coordination bond). Aluminium chloride and AlCl₄⁻ also contain covalent bonds.
items.specStatementText: Coordination bonds are formed when ligands donate an electron pair to transition element cations, forming complex ions.
items.random_wrong: Cu²⁺ donates an electron pair to each H₂O, forming a coordination bond.

items.q: A complex ion contains one Cr³⁺ ion, four H₂O ligands and two Cl⁻ ligands. What is the charge on the complex ion [CrCl₂(H₂O)₄]?
items.why:
Common first examples such as [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ and [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ have neutral ligands, so the complex charge equals the metal ion charge, and students generalize this. Add every charge present: metal ion charge + (number of each ligand × its charge). Neutral ligands (H₂O, NH₃) add 0; anionic ligands (Cl⁻, CN⁻) each add −1. Fe³⁺ + 6CN⁻ → [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻.

Working: Charge on complex = charge on metal ion + sum of ligand charges = (+3) + 2 × (−1) + 4 × 0 = +1, so the ion is [CrCl₂(H₂O)₄]⁺.
items.specStatementText: Coordination bonds are formed when ligands donate an electron pair to transition element cations, forming complex ions.
items.working: Charge on complex = charge on metal ion + sum of ligand charges = (+3) + 2 × (−1) + 4 × 0 = +1, so the ion is [CrCl₂(H₂O)₄]⁺.

items.q: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CBr, reacts with aqueous hydroxide ions by the SN1 mechanism. Which describes the first step?
items.correct: The C–Br bond breaks heterolytically, forming (CH₃)₃C⁺ and Br⁻.
items.misconception: OH⁻ attacks the C atom as the C–Br bond breaks, in a single step.
items.why: The digit in the name is the most visible label, and 'one' and 'two' are naturally read as counts of steps. The meaning of the digit (unimolecular or bimolecular rate-determining step) is easily forgotten. SN2: one concerted step involving two species (halogenoalkane and nucleophile) in the rate-determining step. SN1: two steps, the slow first step involving one species (the halogenoalkane ionizing to a carbocation).
items.specStatementText: Nucleophilic substitution reactions include the reactions between halogenoalkanes and nucleophiles.
items.random_wrong: The C–Br bond breaks homolytically, giving radicals (CH₃)₃C• and Br•.

items.q: A single enantiomer of 2-bromobutane, CH₃CHBrCH₂CH₃, reacts with aqueous hydroxide ions by the SN2 mechanism. Which statement about this reaction is correct?
items.correct: OH⁻ attacks opposite Br, so the configuration is inverted.
items.misconception: OH⁻ takes the exact place of Br, so the configuration is retained.
items.why: Equations such as R–Br → R–OH make substitution look like replacing one label with another, and the word 'substitute' suggests a like-for-like exchange in the same position. Mechanisms show what actually happens. In SN2 the nucleophile must approach the δ+ carbon from the back, away from the leaving group, so the other three groups flip (inversion of configuration). In electrophilic substitution of benzene an intermediate cation forms and then loses H⁺.
items.specStatementText: Nucleophilic substitution reactions include the reactions between halogenoalkanes and nucleophiles.
items.random_wrong: A carbocation forms first, so a racemic mixture is produced.

items.q: Which statement about the mechanisms of nucleophilic substitution of halogenoalkanes is correct?
items.correct: Secondary ones react by SN1 and SN2, as both paths are feasible.
items.misconception: Primary ones react by SN1, as their carbocations are most stable.
items.why: Students expect crowding to be destabilizing, and they treat carbon groups as electron-withdrawing because they know electronegative atoms withdraw electron density. The direction of the alkyl inductive effect is then reversed. Alkyl groups are electron-releasing. Each one pushes electron density toward the positive carbon and helps stabilize it, so (CH₃)₃C⁺ is more stable than (CH₃)₂CH⁺, which is more stable than CH₃CH₂⁺. This is one reason tertiary halogenoalkanes react by SN1 while primary ones react by SN2.
items.specStatementText: Nucleophilic substitution reactions include the reactions between halogenoalkanes and nucleophiles.
items.random_wrong: Tertiary ones react by SN1, which takes place in one step.

items.q: 1-chlorobutane, 1-bromobutane and 1-iodobutane are each warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide under identical conditions. Which reacts fastest, and why?
items.correct: 1-iodobutane, as its C–I bond is the weakest
items.misconception: 1-chlorobutane, as its C–Cl bond is the most polar
items.why: Students have learned that the nucleophile is attracted to the δ+ carbon, so they reason that a larger δ+ must mean a faster reaction, without weighing the bond that has to break. Polarity explains where the nucleophile attacks; bond strength explains how fast the substitution goes. The C–X bond enthalpy falls from C–Cl to C–Br to C–I, so the order of rate is chloroalkane < bromoalkane < iodoalkane, the reverse of the order of polarity.
items.specStatementText: The rate of the substitution reactions is influenced by the identity of the leaving group.
items.random_wrong: 1-chlorobutane, as the small Cl blocks attack least

items.q: Under identical conditions, which reacts faster with aqueous hydroxide ions, 1-bromobutane or 1-chlorobutane, and why?
items.correct: 1-bromobutane, as the C–Br bond is weaker than the C–Cl bond
items.misconception: 1-chlorobutane, as the smaller Cl atom blocks attack less
items.why: Students learn that bulky alkyl groups hinder backside attack in SN2 and apply 'bigger means more hindrance' to the halogen as well. The nucleophile attacks from the side opposite the halogen, so the halogen's size does not block it. What matters for the leaving group is how easily the C–X bond breaks: C–I breaks most easily, so iodoalkanes react fastest.
items.specStatementText: The rate of the substitution reactions is influenced by the identity of the leaving group.
items.random_wrong: 1-chlorobutane, as the C–Cl bond is more polar than C–Br

items.q: Ethene reacts with hydrogen bromide by electrophilic addition. Which describes the curly arrows in the first step of the mechanism?
items.correct: From the C=C bond to the H of HBr, and from the H–Br bond to Br
items.misconception: From the H atom of HBr to the C=C bond, and from Br to the H–Br bond
items.why: Students picture the positive or electron-poor species 'grabbing' electrons and draw the arrow from it toward the electrons, as in the everyday sense of attack. Reversed arrows are among the most commonly reported errors in students' mechanisms. Always start the arrow where the electrons are, at a lone pair or a bond, and end it where they go. For H–Cl → H⁺ + Cl⁻ the arrow goes from the H–Cl bond to Cl; for OH⁻ attacking a halogenoalkane it goes from the O lone pair to the carbon.
items.specStatementText: Alkenes readily undergo electrophilic addition reactions.
items.random_wrong: From the C=C bond to the Br of HBr, and from the H–Br bond to the H

items.q: Ethene reacts with bromine by electrophilic addition. How does the non-polar Br₂ molecule come to act as an electrophile?
items.correct: The electron-rich C=C induces a dipole in Br₂, and Brδ+ accepts the C=C pair.
items.misconception: UV light splits Br₂ into Br atoms, and each Br atom adds to a carbon.
items.why: The first reaction of bromine with a hydrocarbon that students meet is radical substitution of an alkane, which needs UV light to break Br–Br homolytically. The condition is carried over to alkenes. The condition depends on the hydrocarbon. Alkanes need UV light (radical substitution). Alkenes react with Br₂ in the dark at room temperature because the electron-rich C=C bond reacts with Br₂ directly; this is why bromine is used as a test for C=C.
items.specStatementText: Alkenes readily undergo electrophilic addition reactions.
items.random_wrong: Br₂ first ionizes into Br⁺ and Br⁻, and Br⁺ accepts the C=C electron pair.

items.q: In the acid-catalysed addition of water to ethene, the first step forms the carbocation CH₃CH₂⁺. Which describes what happens next?
items.correct: A lone pair on the O of H₂O bonds to C⁺, then H⁺ is lost, regenerating the catalyst.
items.misconception: A lone pair on the O of H₂O bonds to C⁺, and the H⁺ stays, so the acid is used up.
items.why: Catalysts are defined as 'not used up', and students either conclude that a catalyst takes no part in the reaction or, once they see it taking part, that it must be consumed. Both views are commonly reported among chemistry students. A catalyst takes part and is regenerated. In acid-catalysed hydration, H⁺ adds to C=C, water bonds to the carbocation, and the resulting CH₃CH₂OH₂⁺ loses H⁺: the overall equation, CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O → CH₃CH₂OH, contains no H⁺.
items.specStatementText: Alkenes readily undergo electrophilic addition reactions.
items.random_wrong: The C⁺ ion donates an electron pair to the O atom of H₂O, forming a C–O bond.

items.q: Propene, CH₃CH=CH₂, reacts with hydrogen bromide. What is the major product, and why?
items.correct: 2-bromopropane, as it forms via the more stable secondary carbocation
items.misconception: 1-bromopropane, as H adds to the carbon that has fewer H atoms
items.why: Markovnikov's rule is often remembered as a slogan about hydrogen atoms, and the direction is easily reversed, especially when the rule is memorized without the carbocation reasoning behind it. Reason from the intermediate: H⁺ adds to the carbon that gives the more stable carbocation. In propene, H to the CH₂ end gives a secondary carbocation; H to the middle carbon would give a primary one. So H goes to the carbon with MORE H atoms and the major product is 2-bromopropane.
items.specStatementText: The relative stability of carbocations in the addition reactions between hydrogen halides and unsymmetrical alkenes can be used to explain the reaction mechanism.
items.random_wrong: 1-bromopropane, as it forms via the more stable primary carbocation

items.q: 2-methylpropene, (CH₃)₂C=CH₂, reacts with water in the presence of an acid catalyst. What is the major organic product?
items.correct: 2-methylpropan-2-ol, via the tertiary carbocation
items.misconception: A 1:1 mixture of the two possible alcohols
items.why: Students who have met only symmetrical alkenes such as ethene and but-2-ene, where the direction does not matter, assume there is no preference with any alkene. The two directions give different carbocations, and they are not equally stable. The more stable (more substituted) carbocation forms much faster, so its product is the major product: propene + HBr gives mainly 2-bromopropane.
items.specStatementText: The relative stability of carbocations in the addition reactions between hydrogen halides and unsymmetrical alkenes can be used to explain the reaction mechanism.
items.random_wrong: 2-methylpropan-1-ol, as H adds to the C with fewer H

items.q: Which statement about the reaction of benzene with electrophiles is correct?
items.correct: It undergoes substitution; the product keeps the delocalized ring.
items.misconception: It undergoes addition across a C=C bond, in the same way as an alkene.
items.why: The Kekulé structure, still widely drawn, shows benzene with three C=C double bonds, so students treat each as an alkene double bond. Benzene has a delocalized ring of π electrons, not three separate double bonds. The delocalized ring is especially stable, so benzene reacts by substitution, which restores the ring, rather than by addition, which would destroy it.
items.specStatementText: Electrophilic substitution reactions include the reactions of benzene with electrophiles.
items.random_wrong: It does not react at all, as its ring is saturated, like a cycloalkane.

items.q: Benzene reacts with a charged electrophile, E⁺. Which sequence describes the mechanism?
items.correct: Ring π electrons bond to E⁺, forming a cation; loss of H⁺ restores the ring.
items.misconception: Ring π electrons bond to E⁺, forming a cation; a nucleophile then adds to it.
items.why: The Kekulé structure, still widely drawn, shows benzene with three C=C double bonds, so students treat each as an alkene double bond. Benzene has a delocalized ring of π electrons, not three separate double bonds. The delocalized ring is especially stable, so benzene reacts by substitution, which restores the ring, rather than by addition, which would destroy it.
items.specStatementText: Electrophilic substitution reactions include the reactions of benzene with electrophiles.
items.random_wrong: E⁺ donates an electron pair to the ring, forming an anion; H⁻ is then lost.

items.q: 1-bromobutane, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂Br, and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CBr, are each warmed with aqueous hydroxide ions. Which statement about their mechanisms is correct?
items.correct: 1-bromobutane reacts by SN2 in a single step; (CH₃)₃CBr by SN1 via a carbocation
items.misconception: 1-bromobutane reacts by SN2 via a stable intermediate; (CH₃)₃CBr by SN1 via a carbocation
items.why: Drawings of the SN2 transition state in square brackets look like an ordinary structure, so students treat it as a species that exists for a time, like an intermediate. An intermediate sits in an energy minimum between steps; a transition state is at an energy maximum within a step. The SN2 transition state has partial bonds to both the nucleophile and the leaving group and exists only momentarily; there is only one step.
items.specStatementText: Nucleophilic substitution reactions include the reactions between halogenoalkanes and nucleophiles.
items.random_wrong: 1-bromobutane reacts by SN1 via a primary carbocation; (CH₃)₃CBr by SN2 in a single step

items.q: Water can undergo heterolytic fission of one O–H bond to form H⁺ and OH⁻. The diagram shows four attempts, P to S, to draw this change with a curly arrow. Which drawing is correct?
items.correct: Drawing P
items.misconception: Drawing Q
items.why: 'Gaining' is associated with 'plus', and students confuse the sign convention for charge with the idea of gaining something. The same sign confusion appears when oxidation and reduction are described in terms of electrons. Electrons are negative. A fragment that ends up with both bonding electrons has one more electron than it contributed, so it is negative: H–Cl → H⁺ + Cl⁻, with Cl taking the pair.
items.specStatementText: Heterolytic fission is the breakage of a covalent bond when both bonding electrons remain with one of the two fragments formed.
items.random_wrong: Drawing R

items.q: The diagram shows the reactants in the reaction BF₃ + F⁻ → BF₄⁻, with a curly arrow. BF₃ is drawn as a displayed formula; all four lone pairs of F⁻ are shown. Which statement about the reaction is correct?
items.correct: F⁻ is the Lewis base, since it supplies both electrons of the coordination bond
items.misconception: F⁻ is the Lewis acid, since it is the species that donates the electron pair
items.why: In Brønsted–Lowry theory the acid is the donor (of H⁺), so students keep 'acid = donor' and attach it to the electron pair in Lewis theory. The two definitions are in fact complementary: an H⁺ donor is an electron-pair acceptor. Link the two theories through H⁺: H⁺ accepts an electron pair, so it is a Lewis acid. In Lewis terms, acid = electron-pair ACCEPTOR (H⁺, BF₃, AlCl₃, metal cations) and base = electron-pair DONOR (NH₃, H₂O, OH⁻, Cl⁻, C=C).
items.specStatementText: When a Lewis base reacts with a Lewis acid, a coordination bond is formed. Nucleophiles are Lewis bases and electrophiles are Lewis acids.
items.random_wrong: Neither species is an acid or a base, since no H⁺ ion is transferred

items.q: The diagram shows a complex ion of cobalt with its ligands, drawn inside square brackets with the overall charge of the ion outside. What is the charge on the cobalt ion in this complex?
items.why:
Ligands are described as 'electron-pair donors', and electrons are negative, so students assume each ligand contributes negative charge. Donating a pair to share in a bond does not add charge to the complex; charge is conserved. Use the charge each ligand has as a free species: H₂O 0, NH₃ 0, Cl⁻ −1, CN⁻ −1.

Working: Overall charge = charge on metal ion + sum of ligand charges. The diagram shows four NH₃ ligands (each 0), two Cl⁻ ligands (each −1) and an overall charge of +1: +1 = x + 4(0) + 2(−1), so x = +1 + 2 = +3. The ion is [CoCl₂(NH₃)₄]⁺ containing Co³⁺.
items.specStatementText: Coordination bonds are formed when ligands donate an electron pair to transition element cations, forming complex ions.
items.working: Overall charge = charge on metal ion + sum of ligand charges. The diagram shows four NH₃ ligands (each 0), two Cl⁻ ligands (each −1) and an overall charge of +1: +1 = x + 4(0) + 2(−1), so x = +1 + 2 = +3. The ion is [CoCl₂(NH₃)₄]⁺ containing Co³⁺.

items.q: A primary halogenoalkane and a tertiary halogenoalkane each react with aqueous hydroxide ions. The diagram shows the energy profiles, P and Q, of the two reactions. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Q is for the tertiary halogenoalkane, as its dip is the carbocation intermediate
items.misconception: P is for the primary halogenoalkane, as its peak is the intermediate of the reaction
items.why: Both are described as species formed between the reactants and the products, and both are often drawn in square brackets in mechanisms, so students do not separate an energy maximum from an energy minimum on the profile. Match each feature of the profile to a species. A peak is a transition state (partial bonds, cannot be isolated). A dip between two peaks is an intermediate, a real species with a finite lifetime such as the SN1 carbocation. A one-peak profile, as for SN2, has a transition state but no intermediate.
items.specStatementText: Nucleophilic substitution reactions include the reactions between halogenoalkanes and nucleophiles.
items.random_wrong: P is for the tertiary halogenoalkane, as its single peak shows a one-step mechanism

items.q: But-1-ene, CH₃CH₂CH=CH₂, reacts with hydrogen bromide. The diagram shows skeletal formulas of the two carbocations, P and Q, that could form when H⁺ adds to the C=C bond. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: P forms faster, as its positive carbon is stabilized by two electron-releasing alkyl groups
items.misconception: Q forms faster, as its positive carbon has only one electron-withdrawing alkyl group
items.why: Students expect crowding to be destabilizing, and they treat carbon groups as electron-withdrawing because they know electronegative atoms withdraw electron density. The direction of the alkyl inductive effect is then reversed. Alkyl groups are electron-releasing. Each one pushes electron density toward the positive carbon and helps stabilize it, so (CH₃)₃C⁺ is more stable than (CH₃)₂CH⁺, which is more stable than CH₃CH₂⁺. This is one reason tertiary halogenoalkanes react by SN1 while primary ones react by SN2.
items.specStatementText: The relative stability of carbocations in the addition reactions between hydrogen halides and unsymmetrical alkenes can be used to explain the reaction mechanism.
items.random_wrong: Q forms, as the H atom adds to the carbon atom of C=C that has fewer H atoms

items.q: The diagram shows the intermediate formed when benzene reacts with an electrophile, E⁺, together with the curly arrow for the step that follows. What happens in the step shown?
items.correct: The C–H bonding pair moves into the ring, restoring delocalization, and H⁺ is lost
items.misconception: The arrow shows the hydrogen atom moving to another carbon atom of the ring
items.why: In everyday diagrams arrows show objects moving, and in equations arrows point from reactants to products. Curly arrows are therefore read as 'this atom goes there'; treating them as movements of atoms rather than electrons is widely reported in research on students' use of the curly-arrow formalism. A curly arrow shows the movement of TWO electrons: it starts at a lone pair or a bond and ends at the atom (or between atoms) where the pair goes. Atoms move as a consequence, but the arrow does not show them.
items.specStatementText: Electrophilic substitution reactions include the reactions of benzene with electrophiles.
items.random_wrong: A nucleophile adds to the positive carbon, giving an addition product

items.q: In the reaction of 1-bromopropane with aqueous hydroxide ions, does OH⁻ remove a hydrogen ion from the molecule?
items.correct: No. OH⁻ acts as a nucleophile: it donates a lone pair to the carbon bonded to Br, forming propan-1-ol, and Br⁻ leaves.
items.misconception: The hydroxide ion always reacts as a Brønsted–Lowry base, removing H⁺ from whatever it meets.
items.why: OH⁻ is met first and most often in acid–base chemistry as 'the base' that removes H⁺, so students assign it the same role in every reaction. The same species can play different roles. With an acid, OH⁻ accepts H⁺; with a halogenoalkane it donates its lone pair to the δ+ carbon and substitutes for the halogen: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + Br⁻.
items.specStatementText: In a nucleophilic substitution reaction, a nucleophile donates an electron pair to form a new bond, as another bond breaks producing a leaving group.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does 'heterolytic' mean that the bond broken is between two different atoms?
items.correct: No. 'Heterolytic' refers to the unequal split of the bonding electrons, not to the atoms joined. The same bond between different atoms can break either way: the C–Cl bond breaks heterolytically when a nucleophile substitutes for Cl (Cl leaves as Cl⁻), but homolytically in UV light, e.g. CCl₂F₂ → •CClF₂ + Cl•.
items.misconception: Heterolytic fission is the breaking of a bond between two different atoms; homolytic fission is the breaking of a bond between two identical atoms.
items.why: Students know the prefixes hetero- (different) and homo- (same) from terms such as heteronuclear and homonuclear, and apply them to the atoms rather than to the way the electrons are shared out. The standard classroom examples reinforce this: homolysis is shown for Cl–Cl or Br–Br under UV light, heterolysis for H–Br or C–Br. Hetero- and homo- describe the fragments formed. Heterolytic: the two fragments are different, one with both electrons (an anion) and one with none (a cation). Homolytic: the two fragments are alike, each with one electron (radicals).
items.specStatementText: Heterolytic fission is the breakage of a covalent bond when both bonding electrons remain with one of the two fragments formed.

items.q: Do the carbon atoms in an alkene react because they lack a full outer shell?
items.correct: No. Each carbon atom in an alkene already has eight outer electrons. Alkenes react with electrophiles because the C=C double bond is a region of high electron density.
items.misconception: Atoms react in order to complete their octets, so the carbon atoms of C=C react because they need more electrons for a full outer shell.
items.why: The octet rule is taught as the reason atoms bond, and students then use 'atoms want a full shell' to explain every reaction. This octet framework is well documented in chemistry-education research as a source of misconceptions about why reactions occur. Count the electrons: each carbon in C=C shares four pairs, so it already has an octet. The reason alkenes react with electrophiles is the high electron density of the double bond, which attracts electron-pair acceptors.
items.specStatementText: Alkenes are susceptible to electrophilic attack because of the high electron density of the carbon–carbon double bond. These reactions lead to electrophilic addition.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When charges are combined to find the charge on a complex ion, are the signs taken into account?
items.correct: Yes. Charges are added algebraically: (+3) + 2(−1) = +1.
items.misconception: Charges are combined by adding their sizes, ignoring whether they are positive or negative.
items.why: A systematic procedural error when several charged species are combined: the numbers are added and the signs are dropped, as in adding counts of ions. Keep the sign with each charge and add algebraically. For Cr³⁺ with two Cl⁻ and four H₂O: (+3) + 2(−1) + 4(0) = +1.
items.specStatementText: Coordination bonds are formed when ligands donate an electron pair to transition element cations, forming complex ions.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the rate of substitution the same whichever halogen the halogenoalkane contains, because the nucleophile attacks carbon, not the halogen?
items.correct: No. The C–X bond must break during substitution, and its strength depends on the halogen, so the rate changes: iodoalkane > bromoalkane > chloroalkane.
items.misconception: Because the nucleophile attacks the carbon atom, the identity of the halogen does not affect the rate.
items.why: Students focus on bond making (the nucleophile attacking carbon) and overlook the bond that must break, so the leaving group seems irrelevant. Substitution involves making the C–Nu bond AND breaking the C–X bond. The weaker the C–X bond, the faster the reaction, so changing the halogen changes the rate.
items.specStatementText: The rate of the substitution reactions is influenced by the identity of the leaving group.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is benzene unreactive toward electrophiles because it is saturated?
items.correct: No. Benzene is unsaturated and does react with electrophiles, but by substitution rather than addition; for example it is nitrated by NO₂⁺.
items.misconception: Benzene does not react with electrophiles, as it is saturated like a cycloalkane.
items.why: Benzene does not decolorize bromine at room temperature and is described as 'stable', so students conclude that it behaves like a saturated hydrocarbon. Benzene's delocalized π electrons form a region of high electron density that does attract electrophiles. Its stability means it reacts by substitution, keeping the delocalized ring, and needs a strong electrophile such as NO₂⁺.
items.specStatementText: Electrophilic substitution reactions include the reactions of benzene with electrophiles.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the hydration of an alkene add hydrogen to the double bond, forming an alkane?
items.correct: No. Hydration adds water: H to one carbon and OH to the other, forming an alcohol. Adding hydrogen to form an alkane is a different reaction (hydrogenation, with H₂ and a metal catalyst).
items.misconception: Hydration of an alkene adds hydrogen atoms across the double bond, so water converts an alkene into an alkane.
items.why: 'Hydration' and 'hydrogenation' sound alike, and both are addition reactions of alkenes, so the two names and their products are easily confused. Hydration = adding H₂O (alkene → alcohol, e.g. but-2-ene → butan-2-ol). Hydrogenation = adding H₂ (alkene → alkane). The reagent's name tells you what is added.
items.specStatementText: Alkenes are susceptible to electrophilic attack because of the high electron density of the carbon–carbon double bond. These reactions lead to electrophilic addition.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In nucleophilic substitution, is the new bond to the nucleophile made from the electrons of the carbon–halogen bond that breaks?
items.correct: No. The C–X bonding pair leaves with the halogen as X⁻; the new C–Nu bond is made from an electron pair donated by the nucleophile.
items.misconception: Substitution is a swap of groups on one bond: the C–X bonding pair stays on the carbon and is simply handed over to the incoming nucleophile.
items.why: Equations such as CH₃CH₂Br → CH₃CH₂OH look like one label being exchanged for another on the same bond, and the everyday meaning of 'substitute' suggests a like-for-like exchange rather than one bond breaking and a different bond forming. Two electron pairs move: a lone pair of the nucleophile forms the new C–Nu bond, and the C–X bonding pair moves onto X, which leaves as X⁻. In CH₃CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂OH + Br⁻ the C–O pair comes from O and the C–Br pair leaves with Br⁻.
items.specStatementText: In a nucleophilic substitution reaction, a nucleophile donates an electron pair to form a new bond, as another bond breaks producing a leaving group.
